lede: CULTURA X NATUREZA = BARBÁRIE - The animal is foreign par excellence, the truly incomprehensible other.
about.0:
CULTURE X NATURE = BARBA-
RISM - Animals are foreign par
excellence, the truly incomprehensible other. The equation looks complete: “Culture
versus Nature = Barbarism”
(1997-2004). At the end, two
incompatible elements provoke
destruction. In a way, the artist
seems to place before our eyes
the negative of the romantic
dream that Beuys represented,
his confidence in the possibility of utilizing animal energy
to arrive at that desired state
of unity that Schiller, for example, had already exalted much
earlier in expressing his envy of
the Greeks’ proximity to nature:
“they are that which we were,
that which we must return to
being. Like them, we have been
nature, and our culture must
follow the path of reason and
freedom back to nature.”
Mercedes Replinger González, extract from the book Instalações Barja - 2005; from the text “Uncertain documents in place of the monster”.

This is especially true when the nomenclature forms part of the work, and the naming has a determinant function in a triangle of verbal, conceptual and visual powers. Many of these works, in fact, start working when this verbal-visual element is activated, generating a multiple aesthetic force field where even the sensorial territory is produced by conceptual and reflexive contiguity. It’s in this sense that Da², H2O- Monet, Fike and even Natureza X Cultura = Barbárie stand concerted. trecho.5: a, for other (many) uses… Something like: The Submerged Eyes: submerging objects in water and exposing them to their lookers. An optical operation of distortion of the image, a symbolic operation of displacement of meanings, an operation of dismantling the work in its own construction (it is there, precarious, on the verge of undoing itself for harbouring what cannot occupy the same place — water and electricity — since the submerged image shows itself on TV screens). These aquarium-boxes, which carry other boxes (aquarium?), produce their own equation, which the artist formulates as natureza X cultura = barbárie, his own formulation of circularity: who looks at whom? Who is the referent? Where does the proposal begin? And is this not the equation without an answer produced by art, at the very least since Velasquez? The opaque eyes of “Hermógenes”: the story of being presented to the world by a blind grandfather may imply the habit of “guessing sight” or of exercising it with closed eyes, reinventing the world. The story of recalling the world (through reading) to a blind grandfather may imply a re-elaboration of things through the word, a certain subjection of reality to another (also) imaginary order. The concreteness (and the ephemerality) of letters: the idea of “eating” ideas has belonged to us since the beginning of the twentieth century, when the native custom of anthropophagy was metaphorized, at the time of the discovery of the new world: we eat people, we eat cultures, we live the fantasy of leaving barbarism (animality) behind by swallowing what we wanted and what we did not want. Acknowledging the ancestry both of the masters of 22 and of what Brazilian concrete poetry teaches, two objects/visual poems, DO AKAD-MICO AO POLE-MICO, play at undoing both the “law” of artistic (and of thought) production and its contestation. As promise and threat, the mico (in flesh, bone and figurative sense) aligns itself with the bananas that form the two prefixes, already asserting its ephemerality (its destiny is as clear as the gaze the mico casts upon them). Barja, at a given moment, finds himself before the contingency of hearing, from the movement’s great theorist, the assertion of the “death of art”. His commentary-response is a work/mausoleum, a declaration of disagreement through the establishment of a play of mirrors in which the prophecy turns back upon whoever pronounces it. The irony of the ensemble itself questions the purpose of the oratory, in the museum and in the church: art as a means of healing. Art does not heal wounds. Barja does not seem to believe in the redemptive or emancipatory capacities of contemporary art and science. Between what man thinks, desires, even imagines and what he is by nature, there is no correspondence. The animal is foreign par excellence, the truly incomprehensible other. The equation appears complete: “Cultura X Natureza = Barbárie” (1997 -2004). At the end, two incompatible elements provoke destruction.
